paragraphs: “Do you want me to bow down to you, monk?” said Father Ferapont. “Get up!”
The monk got up.
“Blessing, be blessed! Sit down beside me. Where have you come from?”

What struck the poor monk most was that, for all his strict fasting and great age, Father Ferapont still looked like a vigorous old man. He was tall and held himself straight, and his face was thin but fresh and healthy. There was no doubt he still had considerable strength. He was built like an athlete. Despite his great age he was not even completely gray. His hair was still very thick and his beard full, and both had once been black. His eyes were gray, large and bright, but strikingly prominent. He spoke with a broad accent. He wore a peasant’s long reddish coat of coarse convict cloth (as it used to be called), with a stout rope round his waist. His throat and chest were bare. Under the coat, his shirt of the coarsest linen looked almost black with dirt, since it had not been changed for months. They said he wore irons weighing thirty pounds under his coat. His bare feet were thrust into old slippers that were almost falling to pieces.
“From the little Obdorsk monastery, from St. Sylvester,” the monk answered humbly, while his keen, inquisitive but rather frightened little eyes kept watch on the hermit.
“I’ve been at your Sylvester’s. I used to stay there. Is Sylvester well?”
The monk hesitated.
“You’re a senseless lot! How do you keep the fasts?”

“Our diet follows the ancient rules of the monastery. In Lent, no meals are provided on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. On Tuesday and Thursday we have white bread, stewed fruit with honey, wild berries, or salted cabbage and porridge made of coarse meal. On Saturday we have white cabbage soup, noodles with peas, and kasha, all with hemp oil. On weekdays we have dried fish and kasha with the cabbage soup. From Monday until Saturday evening, six whole days in Holy Week, nothing is cooked. We have only bread and water, and that sparingly, and if possible we do not eat every day, exactly as is ordered for the first week of Lent. On Good Friday nothing is eaten. In the same way on the Saturday we fast until three o’clock, and then take a little bread and water and drink a single cup of wine. On Holy Thursday we drink wine and have something cooked without oil, or not cooked at all, since the council of Laodicea lays down for Holy Thursday: ‘It is unseemly to dishonor the whole of Lent by relaxing the fast on Holy Thursday!’ This is how we keep the fast. But what is that compared with you, holy Father,” added the monk, growing more confident, “for all the year round, even at Easter, you take nothing but bread and water, and what we would eat in two days lasts you a full seven. Your great abstinence is truly marvelous.”
“And mushrooms?” Father Ferapont asked suddenly.
“Mushrooms?” repeated the surprised monk.

“Yes. I can give up their bread, because I don’t need it at all, and go off into the forest and live on mushrooms or berries. But they can’t give up their bread here, and that is why they are in bondage to the devil. These days the unclean deny that there is any need for such fasting. Their judgment is proud and unclean.”
“Och, true,” sighed the monk.
“And have you seen devils among them?” asked Ferapont.
“Among them? Among whom?” asked the monk timidly.

“I went to the Father Superior on Trinity Sunday last year, and I haven’t been since. I saw a devil sitting on one man’s chest, hiding under his cassock, with only his horns poking out. Another had one peeping out of his pocket, with such sharp eyes, he was afraid of me. Another had settled in somebody’s unclean belly. Another was hanging round a man’s neck, and so the man was carrying him about without seeing him.”
“You—can see spirits?” the monk asked.

“I tell you I can see, I can see right through them. When I was coming out from the Superior’s I saw one hiding from me behind the door, and a big one, a yard and a half or more high, with a thick long gray tail. The tip of his tail was in the crack of the door, and I was quick and slammed the door, pinching his tail in it. He squealed and began to struggle, and I made the sign of the cross over him three times. And he died on the spot like a crushed spider. He must have rotted there in the corner and be stinking by now, but they don’t see it, they don’t smell it. It’s a year since I’ve been there. I’m telling you this because you’re a stranger.”

“Your words are terrible! But, holy and blessed Father,” said the monk, growing bolder and bolder, “is it true, as they spread about even to distant lands, that you are in continual communication with the Holy Ghost?”
“He does fly down at times.”
“How does he fly down? In what form?”
“As a bird.”
“The Holy Ghost in the form of a dove?”
“There’s the Holy Ghost and there’s the Holy Spirit. The Holy Spirit can appear as other birds—sometimes as a swallow, sometimes a goldfinch, sometimes a blue-tit.”
“How do you tell him from an ordinary tit?”
“He speaks.”
“How does he speak, in what language?”
“Human language.”
“And what does he tell you?”
“Why, today he told me that a fool would visit me and ask me improper questions. You want to know too much, monk.”
“Your words are terrible, most holy and blessed Father,” the monk said, shaking his head. But there was a doubtful look in his frightened little eyes.
“Do you see this tree?” asked Father Ferapont, after a pause.
“I do, blessed Father.”
“You think it’s an elm, but to me it has another shape.”
“What sort of shape?” asked the monk, after waiting in vain for more.
“It happens at night. You see those two branches? At night it is Christ holding out His arms to me and seeking me with those arms. I see it clearly and tremble. It’s terrible, terrible!”
“What’s terrible about it, if it’s Christ Himself?”
“Why, He’ll snatch me up and carry me away.”
“Alive?”
“In the spirit and glory of Elijah, haven’t you heard? He will take me in His arms and bear me away.”

The monk went back to the cell he was sharing with one of the brothers in considerable perplexity. Still, in his heart he had greater reverence for Father Ferapont than for Father Zossima. He was strongly in favor of fasting, and it was not strange to him that a man who kept so rigid a fast as Father Ferapont should “see marvels.” The words certainly seemed queer, but God alone could tell what was hidden in them. And weren’t worse words and deeds commonly seen in people who have sacrificed their minds for the glory of God? As for the pinching of the devil’s tail, he was ready and eager to believe it, and not only in a figurative sense. Besides, before visiting the monastery he had held a strong prejudice against the institution of “elders.” He knew it only by hearsay and believed it to be a harmful innovation. Before he had been long at the monastery, he had picked up on the secret grumbling of some shallow brothers who disliked the institution. He was also a meddlesome, inquisitive man who poked his nose into everything. This was why the news of the fresh “miracle” performed by Father Zossima threw him into extreme perplexity. Alyosha remembered afterwards how their inquisitive guest from Obdorsk had been flitting continually from one group to another, listening and asking questions among the monks who were crowding in and around the elder’s cell. But he did not pay much attention to him at the time, and only recalled it afterwards.

Indeed, he had no thought to spare for it. Father Zossima had felt tired again and gone back to bed, and as he was closing his eyes he thought of Alyosha and sent for him. Alyosha ran to him at once. There was no one else in the cell but Father Païssy, Father Iosif, and the novice Porfiry. The elder opened his weary eyes, looked intently at Alyosha, and suddenly asked him:
“Are your people expecting you, my son?”
Alyosha hesitated.
“Don’t they need you? Didn’t you promise someone yesterday that you would see them today?”
“I did promise—to my father—my brothers—others too.”

“You see, you must go. Don’t grieve. Be sure I will not die without your being there to hear my last word. I will say that word to you, my son, it will be my last gift to you. To you, dear son, because you love me. But now go and keep your promise.”

Alyosha obeyed at once, though it was hard to go. But the promise that he would hear the elder’s last word on earth, and that it would be a last gift to him, Alyosha, sent a thrill of rapture through his soul. He hurried, so that he could finish what he had to do in the town and return quickly. Father Païssy, too, spoke some words of exhortation that moved and greatly surprised him. He spoke as they left the cell together.

“Remember, young man, always,” Father Païssy began, without any preface, “that the science of this world has become a great power. Especially in the last century, it has analyzed everything divine that was handed down to us in the holy books. After this cruel analysis the learned of this world have nothing left of all that was once sacred. But they have analyzed only the parts and overlooked the whole, and their blindness is truly marvelous. Yet the whole still stands steadfast before their eyes, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it. Has it not lasted nineteen centuries? Is it not still a living, moving power in the individual soul and in the masses of the people? It is still as strong and alive even in the souls of atheists, who have destroyed everything! For even those who have renounced Christianity and attack it still follow the Christian ideal in their inmost being. Until now, neither their cleverness nor the ardor of their hearts has been able to create a higher ideal of man and of virtue than the ideal given by Christ long ago. When it has been attempted, the result has been only grotesque. Remember this above all, young man, since your departing elder is sending you into the world. Perhaps, when you remember this great day, you will not forget my words, spoken from the heart for your guidance. You are young, and the temptations of the world are great and beyond your strength to endure. Well, now go, my orphan.”

With these words Father Païssy blessed him. As Alyosha left the monastery and thought them over, he suddenly realized that in this austere monk, who until now had treated him sternly, he had found a new and unexpected friend, a warmly loving teacher. It was as though Father Zossima had left him to Father Païssy at his death, and “perhaps that’s just what had passed between them,” Alyosha thought suddenly. The philosophical reflections he had just heard so unexpectedly showed the warmth of Father Païssy’s heart. He was in a hurry to arm the boy’s mind for the fight against temptation, and to guard the young soul left in his charge with the strongest defense he could imagine.
